1:
The prophet who was told to comfort is now told to convict, and Henry marks the reversal: conviction must prepare for comfort, and must also separate the precious from the vile. The command is to spare nobody. Henry hears in it an instruction not to spare the people, not to touch the wound gently but to search it to the bottom, and not to spare the preacher either, though he spend his strength and earn ill will. Ellicott reads the Hebrew literally as crying with the throat, no faint whisper from stammering lips but the full strength of the voice, and takes the trumpet of the next clause as pressing the point further. Clarke says no louder cry was ever raised against a people professing an established religion with all the forms of godliness and not a particle of its power.

What makes the reproof difficult is that the people are devout. They seek God daily, delight to know his ways, ask his ordinances of justice, and take pleasure in drawing near. Gill allows it as genuine external piety, or else as a caution to the prophet not to be imposed on by appearances, but adds that they sought themselves and the honour of men rather than God and his glory. Wesley reads each clause as a pretence: as if they were a righteous people, guilty of no apostasy, resolved to keep the ordinances they asked after. Ellicott finds every phrase ringing with incisive irony, naming one element after another of a true devotion the people did not possess.

Then the worshippers speak, and the complaint is that God has not noticed. Henry hears Cain in it, a man angry that his offering was refused, and observes how they magnify what they have done and expect God to stand in their debt for it. Keil and Delitzsch call this the work-holy delusion, fasting turned from a means of worship into a thing supposed to merit reward, with self-righteousness and unrighteousness concealed behind it. The answer given is not doctrinal but factual: on the day of the fast they carry on their business and press their labourers. Clarke, who has watched it done, says some keep a servant working all day and others use the fast to settle accounts and post their books, the first daringly irreligious and the second sneaking hypocrites.

The fast also breeds quarrels. Henry supposes that a day meant for searching out the sins that provoked the judgment became a day for accusing one another, each party crying that the other had delayed the deliverance, so that instead of judging themselves they condemned their neighbours; nor did the quarrels stop at the tongue. Ellicott offers a different account of the same fact, that unspiritual fasting frets the nerves and embitters the temper, and that the disputes of fasting controversialists are often as fierce as those of drunken ones. Clarke leaves the Hebrew here for the Greek, which he thinks gives the better sense, reading the blow as struck against the poor and the question as why they fast to God in such a manner; few letters separate the two readings.

So the last question is put. Ellicott traces the phrase about afflicting the soul to the law of atonement, where it names a real soul-sorrow, and sets against it the mechanical prostration that is only a bulrush in the breeze. Henry presses the same image: hanging the head like a withered rush is what the hypocrites did who disfigured their faces to be seen fasting; it fitted the publican, whose heart was actually broken, but as mimicry it deserves the ridicule it gets. Sackcloth and ashes may make a man uneasy for the day and be forgotten when he stretches himself again on his bed of ivory. Wesley calls it a fast with nothing in it but the dumb signs of one.
6:
The answer comes as a list of things to be undone: bands of wickedness loosed, burdens lifted, the oppressed set free, every yoke broken. Keil and Delitzsch say the fasting God likes is not abstinence as such but the self-denying love that gives up bread for the sake of the needy, and they hear a bitter irony in it, matching an old saying that not eating is a natural fast while abstaining from sin is the spiritual one. Ellicott will not let the verse abolish what it corrects: the words do not exclude abstinence as discipline, they declare its insufficiency by itself. He gives the heavy burdens their literal sense, the leather thongs that fastened the yoke to the ploughing ox's head.

Two commentators reach independently for the same history. During the siege, Keil and Delitzsch recall, the slaves of Israelite descent were freed by public resolution, and as soon as the besiegers withdrew their masters fetched them back into servitude; the same despotic temper went with them into captivity. Ellicott calls it a truth recognised in the hour of danger and forgotten in that of safety. Clarke will not keep it in the past. How can any nation pretend to worship God, he demands, or dare to profess that it believes such a Being exists, while it carries on the slave trade and traffics in the souls, blood and bodies of men. Better to cast off the mask of religion than deepen perdition by professing the faith while continuing in that traffic.

The charity required is equally concrete. Gill notes that the word is to break the bread rather than give it, and that it must be one's own and not another's, saved by the fasting rather than laid up. Clarke draws the arithmetic out: a man who fasts should give that day's food, or its value, to the poor who keep involuntary fasts all year; woe to him who saves a day's victuals by his religion. Ellicott hears the familiar phrase of the breaking of bread, and explains that the thin oval cakes were naturally broken rather than cut. He reads the poor that are cast out as covering every kind of homelessness: tenants evicted by landlords, debtors by creditors, slaves fleeing cruelty, the persecuted, perhaps political refugees.

Hiding from one's own flesh draws the widest comment. Ellicott grants that usage points first to suffering Israelites, but says those who have learned that God made all nations of one blood will extend it to every form of suffering humanity. Wesley refuses the narrow reading: some confine it to our own kindred, but we can look on no man without contemplating our own flesh, so that it is barbarous not merely to tear him but to fail to love him. His rule is a chain of substitutions: feed him as thou wouldest feed thyself, shelter him as thou wouldest be sheltered, clothe him as thou wouldest be clothed. Gill alone turns the bread spiritual as well, the gospel dealt to the hungry rather than consciences burdened with rites of men's devising, husks and not bread.

Then the promises. Wesley reads the light plainly as happiness and prosperity, breaking forth as the sun pierces a cloud, the righteousness going before as the morning star goes before the sun and the glory behind as the angel that secured the people coming out of Egypt. Gill reads the same light as chiefly spiritual and still future, the gospel shining out when persecution yields to love. Henry keeps it near at hand, mercy after long affliction, and adds that the two escorts leave the righteous safe whichever way they look. Clarke reports an old version reading that the scar of the wound shall be speedily removed. The answering voice is what strikes Henry most: that God should say to us, Behold me, here I am, he calls strange.
10:
Drawing out the soul to the hungry is an odd phrase. Clarke says so: it occurs nowhere else, and many manuscripts read thy bread instead. He decides against them. To draw out the soul in relieving the poor is to do it not of constraint but cheerfully, an expression he calls both nervous and elegant and sums up in a line, his soul pities and his hand gives. Ellicott sets out three senses — surrendering sensuous desire, ministering of one's substance, extending sympathy — and prefers the third. Wesley takes the verb as opening, as a store is opened to supply want. Gill adds the preachers who impart not the gospel only but their own souls with it.

The promises that follow are read with an eye on the wilderness. Gill has God guiding as the pillar of cloud and fire guided by day and night, and notes that the verb may also be rendered as giving rest, from adversity now and eternally hereafter. Wesley makes the guide a shepherd and presses the word continually, the blessing not momentary but all along, his unfailing spring set against the brook a drought soon dries up. Ellicott prefers to strengthen or make supple for the promise about the bones, and notes that the drought is plural, either intensive or meaning dry places. Clarke, unsatisfied with a Latin rendering that has God delivering the bones and makes no sense, adopts an emendation giving renewed strength, and reports an old paraphrase promising the body life eternal.

On the rebuilding the commentators divide by scope. Gill runs three applications together: the returned captives who raised the ruined cities, the apostles who repaired the fallen tabernacle after long corruption in doctrine and worship, and a later company who will build the world's waste places, where there has been no preaching and no church. Ellicott keeps the primary sense architectural, the buildings of Jerusalem, and takes the foundations of many generations as ruins lying bare longer than the exile itself. The last clause splits them. Ellicott makes the paths the streets of the city, flanked once more with houses rather than roads from point to point; Wesley makes them the highways between cities, grown over with grass and weeds.

The sabbath section begins with a question of identification. Henry notes that some take this day to be the annual atonement, the fast they suppose the earlier verses mean, and answers that since those fasts were occasional this one is doubtless the weekly sabbath. He reads its restraints strictly: not to walk in our own ways is not to follow our callings, not to find our own pleasure is not to follow our sports, and we may not speak our own words. Clarke applies it to visits and country jaunts, complaining how vilely his countrymen transgress the rule, as though the day were made only for their recreation. Ellicott dissents on the word itself, rendering it thy business rather than thy pleasure, and hears in the turning of the foot the idea of holy ground no profane step may tread.

Gill lists the objects of the delight: the divine perfections, the relations God takes to his people, his works, his word, communion with him. Henry makes the reward internal first, the work its own wages: the more pleasure we take in serving God the more we find in it. The riding on high places he takes as dignity as well as safety, recalling the phrase used of the people led from Egypt. Ellicott would read of the land rather than of the earth, a victorious march occupying the commanding positions of Canaan and joining the heritage promised next. Clarke ends by turning the chapter on his own age, at a nation fasting in 1823 to subjugate its neighbour and restore the inquisition, and asking whether that is the fast God has chosen.
